Les défenseurs des terres ont été convié: Land defenders were invited to take part in the discussions at COP15. But how far does that participation really go?
« Haouthli, les terres et les eaux auxqu: “Haouthli, the lands and waters to which we belong.” Photo: Aya Clappis
Nii Lax Aks, aussi appelé Denzel Sutherl: Nii Lax Aks, also known as Denzel Sutherland-Wilson, is Gitxsan. He was part of the group of young Indigenous people from the West Coast who travelled to the 15th United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15), held in Montréal from December 7 to 19, 2022.
Ces jeunes sont allés témoigner de leurs: These young people went to speak about their work reoccupying their territories and about how Indigenous sovereignty protects biodiversity. To prepare for the trip, Nii Lax Aks gathered cedar in the forest to make smudge sticks. Aya Clappis, who is of Somali and Huu-ay-aht heritage, was also part of the group as a panellist. “I’m here because where I come from, the lands and waters are threatened by industry and governments,” says Aya.
L’accord final de la COP15 comporte un o: The final COP15 agreement includes a target of protecting 30% of the planet’s land, waters and marine areas by 2030. That is the target scientists had been campaigning for, and it is the minimum threshold needed to <l1>halt global biodiversity loss and protect the Earth’s capacity</l1> to support complex life. “When governments talk about <l2>conserving 30% of the land,</l2> what they’re really doing is giving themselves permission to keep helping themselves to the rest,” Nii Lax Aks argues.
En écoutant ces jeunes défenseurs des te: Listening to these young land defenders, one has to grasp the meaning they give to the word “land.” Nii Lax Aks, who is Gitxsan, prefers to use the word “Lax’yip.” Lax’yip does not refer to something an individual can own. “It’s something that is shared among all of us, including with other species and with those who come before us and after us,” he explains. That is very different from the capitalist view, which holds that land is an inanimate object for humans to control.
Parallèlement, la biodiversité est consi: At the same time, biodiversity is seen as an inseparable part of life, and of ourselves, as Willo Prince, who is Nak’azdli Whut’en, points out. “We can’t talk about it as if we were separate from it, because it’s in that separation and that distinction that all these problems lie. Colonization lies in that separation; capitalism lies in that distinction,” says Willo.
Dans le processus d’assimilation, Nii La: In the process of assimilation, Nii Lax Aks denounces “the erasure of our own governance and our philosophies.” “There are a lot of Indigenous leaders who also believe the land has to be controlled and exploited,” he adds. That belief leads to the idea that resources must be extracted and exploited for our presence on, or our relationship with, the land to count. This way of seeing things played a central role in the Delgamuukw v. British Columbia case, 25 years ago. “The decision in that case only half-recognized our belonging to our Lax’yip, and not the way industry operates on the land,” Nii Lax Aks recalls.
Le jeune homme pense à son grand-père, q: The young man thinks of his grandfather, who selectively logged trees using horses. Today, walking through the forest, he sees the mossy stumps still standing there, in the middle of a magnificent, healthy and diverse forest, where his ancestors harvested trees for thousands of years.

« Notre inclusion a été limitée », expos: “Our inclusion was limited,” says Nii Lax Aks. He describes rooms that held 25 to 30 people. “We were given half the time and half the capacity of everyone else. Meanwhile, everyone is saying we need Indigenous leadership, Indigenous knowledge and Indigenous solutions to these problems.”
Willo Prince abonde dans le même sens :: Willo Prince agrees: “That’s true. But it isn’t the whole truth. We can’t just settle for having our world views and teachings taken from us, without that coming with an end to colonial violence on our lands. That’s just another form of extraction. It’s another form of whitewashing. It’s another form of erasure.”
Pour Willo, il est impératif d’aborder l: For Willo, it is imperative to address the following themes: “Colonial violence and Indigenous world views in the fight against climate change.” Otherwise, there will be consequences, Willo continues: “The governments of this federal state could avoid being held accountable.”
« Réfléchissez un instant à ce à quoi re: “Think for a moment about what forests would look like today if reciprocal relationships guided logging. The ability of Indigenous nations to properly steward their forests has been hindered by Canada, which is actively trying to destroy Indigenous thought and spirituality,” Nii Lax Aks continues.
« C’est en se disant la vérité que l’on: “It’s by telling each other the truth that we gain greater awareness, and that’s how we come to acceptance,” Willo Prince believes. “It’s acceptance of everything that may have happened, but also of what could be. And it’s only with that kind of awareness that we’re able to dream, to hope and to envision.”

La Déclaration des Nations unies sur les: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) has been seen as a promising sign “on the path” to reconciliation, reparations and justice. Nii Lax Aks warns against any “instrument of false hope” used to keep people complacent. “The idea that these rights come from an international forum, rather than from our responsibilities, our ancestors, our connection and our intuition, can potentially be harmful, or paralyzing,” he says.
Pour sa part, Aya Clappis n’attend pas q: For her part, Aya Clappis isn’t waiting for Canada to grant her rights to live with and on her ancestral lands and waters. “My birthrights come from thousands of years of caring for our haouthli and taking on our responsibilities toward everything in it,” says Aya. “Haouthli” translates as the lands and waters to which the huuas (Indigenous peoples) belong – and so refers to a broader concept than that of territory.
« Depuis combien de temps nous donnent-i: “How long have they been giving us a little bit of hope?” asks Nii Lax Aks. “I feel like when they sense the land slipping away from them, they give us a glimmer of hope,” he says. “It’s completely understandable that people turn to UNDRIP for protection, because of all the violence and criminalization we’ve faced. But I don’t see it on the ground. We’re on the front lines, where UNDRIP should be acting, to bring about change.”
Nii Lax Aks s’est lui-même retrouvé dans: Nii Lax Aks has himself been in situations where the RCMP apparently paid it no mind. “Officers yelled at me, ‘UNDRIP is not the law!’ Then they went ahead and arrested and removed Indigenous people from their lands,” he recounts.
Témoins de la grande réunion des nations: Witnesses to the great gathering of nations and corporations at COP15, the land defenders were also there to disrupt the status quo. When Prime Minister Justin Trudeau spoke of “our beautiful lands,” the young Indigenous people responded by drumming. They were able to leave freely and, as Nii Lax Aks points out, UN security avoided responding with force. “They wouldn’t do it in front of the whole world,” he says.
Une fois sortis de la salle, les partici: Once out of the room, the participants were pursued by security. They responded again with their drums, before finding the exit. Nii Lax Aks says that shortly after Mr. Trudeau had invoked freedom of expression in Canada, the group was surrounded by the RCMP. They were not arrested, but “detained for investigation.”
Un agent a porté la main vers son arme e: One officer reached toward his weapon, asking: “What do you have in your hand? What’s in your hand?” “It’s cedar,” replied Nii Lax Aks, who was holding his smudge stick.
Il raconte que les membres du groupe ont: He says the members of the group kept drumming while slowly making their way toward where they were staying. Once there, friends opened the door for them, and they slipped inside, away from the RCMP.
Nii Lax Aks tire du réconfort de son rap: Nii Lax Aks draws comfort from his relationship with Lax’yip, which is vast, abundant and capable of healing. “Our ancestors developed all kinds of knowledge about the animals, plants, minerals and other natural forces that sustained them. That knowledge is necessary to live in balance with the land. It can increase abundance and could be the catalyst for profound change,” he explains.
« Pour aller de l’avant, il ne s’agit pa: “Moving forward isn’t about pushing responsibility off into the future, but about taking it on in the present, and understanding that we are first and foremost accountable to Indigenous law, which is natural law,” says Aya Clappis.
Lorsque les défenseurs de la terre parle: When land defenders talk about reoccupying the land, taking back the role of our ancestors and stewarding it, they mean managing it in a way that fosters an abundance of food for humans and other animals through balanced relationships. “To have good relationships with the rest of the world, you have to have a good relationship with the land and be an integral part of it,” says Nii Lax Aks.
Revenant sur le concept de <em>Lax’yip</: Returning to the concept of Lax’yip – a place where different worlds made up of different peoples and species coexist and nourish one another – Nii Lax Aks says: “Our ancestral knowledge holds that animals have their own societies, their own laws and their own consciousness. Those laws were taught to us at some point. There are a lot of people in our community who still believe in that knowledge, who hold it and who use it when they’re out on the territory.”
« Aujourd’hui, nous sommes à un point où: “Today, we’re at a point where I hear the whole world saying this is what we need. The question is whether it will be respected,” says Nii Lax Aks. “But how sincere is this call to action?” he asks in closing.
